stdout_tail:
**Finding:** SMOTE oversampling does **not** meaningfully change minority-class (>50K) F1 for a default RandomForestClassifier on this dataset. F1 went from 0.6795 (no resampling) to 0.6730 (with SMOTE) — a difference of **-0.0065**, well under the 0.02 threshold specified in H5.

Details:
- 75/25 stratified train/test split; median/most-frequent imputation for missing values (`?` and NaN), one-hot encoding for categoricals, preprocessing fit once and shared across both arms for a fair comparison.
- SMOTE applied only to the encoded training set (never the test set), balancing the training class counts from 27,866/8,765 to 27,866/27,866.
- Both arms use `RandomForestClassifier()` with library defaults and the same `random_state=42`.

Results and code are saved to `result.json` and `analysis.py` in the working directory.

parsed_result.summary: Applying SMOTE changed the >50K-class F1 score from 0.6795 (no resampling) to 0.6730 (with SMOTE), a difference of -0.0065. This does not exceed the 0.02 threshold, so SMOTE does not meaningfully change minority-class F1 for a default-hyperparameter random forest on this dataset.
parsed_result.direction: |diff| <= 0.02: SMOTE does not move F1 by more than 0.02 (reduces it)
parsed_result.methodological_choices: 75/25 stratified train/test split (random_state=42); literal '?' strings recoded as NaN alongside existing NaNs; numeric features median-imputed, categorical features most-frequent-imputed then one-hot encoded (unknown categories ignored at test time); preprocessing pipeline fit once on the training set and reused for both conditions so the only difference between arms is SMOTE; SMOTE (imbalanced-learn, random_state=42, default k_neighbors=5) applied only to the encoded training data, never to the test set; RandomForestClassifier used with library-default hyperparameters (n_estimators=100) in both arms, random_state=42; F1 computed for the >50K (minority, pos_label=1) class on the held-out test set; threshold for 'meaningful change' taken as |ΔF1| > 0.02 per the research question.
